title: Kernel observability SLAs and profiling cadence
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary

This page defines a pragmatic, operationally focused observability SLA for the serving runtime kernel layer and specifies a profiling cadence and playbook for keeping kernel regressions visible and remediable. The goal is to ensure kernel-level performance signals (latency, dispatch/backpressure, memory pressure, and kernel success rates) are actionable by oncall and engineering, tied to benchmarking experiments, and budgeted within profiling cost constraints.

Why this matters

- Kernel regressions are the root cause of the majority of hard-to-diagnose tail-latency incidents.
- Observability at the kernel boundary is expensive; we need a cost-aware sampling strategy and a clear schedule so telemetry budgets are predictable.
- Tying profiling to the benchmarking suite and release gates reduces the chance of regressing a deployment unnoticed.

Scope

This document covers the manifest, SLOs, sampling & tracing cadence, profiling runbook, integration points with the benchmarking suite and release process, and known limitations. It applies to:

- The inference runtime kernel components (dispatcher, scheduler, kernel executor, KV cache interface).
- Host-level telemetry produced by kernel shim and GPU-side counters that we ingest via the kernel agent.

Key definitions

- Kernel sample: a single end-to-end kernel execution record (dispatch -> kernel launch -> completion) including timestamps, kernel variant id, request classification, memory footprint, and outcome code.
- Observability SLA: the target for alertable metrics derived from kernel samples (e.g., kernel_p99_duration, kernel_error_rate).
- Profiling window: an intentional time-bounded full-capture session used for deep analysis (trace-level).

Observability SLA (metrics and thresholds)

Table: metric | alert threshold | target (SLO) | runbook severity
- kernel_p95_execution_ms | > 80ms sustained 5m | SLO: p95 < 60ms over 24h | Sev2
- kernel_p99_execution_ms | > 200ms sustained 5m | SLO: p99 < 150ms over 24h | Sev1
- kernel_error_rate (non-transient) | > 0.5% over 10m | SLO: < 0.2% | Sev1
- kernel_dispatch_queue_depth | > 200 for 1m | SLO: median < 50 | Sev2
- kernel_memory_pressure_evictions_per_min | > 1/min | SLO: < 0.1/min | Sev2

Notes: thresholds are intentionally tighter than product-level SLA to detect regressions earlier. Alerting rules are configured in Monitoring (Grafana/Prometheus) under team "runtime-kernel-observability". Alerts map to runbook escalation in the Runbooks section.

Sampling policy and retention budget

- Continuous aggregated metrics: emitted for all kernels (high-cardinality fields are hashed). Retained for 90 days.
- Detailed traces (span-level, per-request kernels): sampled using hybrid sampling: deterministic sampling for top 1% traffic cohorts by token volume + probabilistic reservoir sampling (0.5% of all requests) to ensure long-tail visibility.
- Profiling windows (full capture): scheduled 3 times per week in production canaries and once weekly in a matched staging shard. Each profiling window is limited to 15 minutes per shard to keep cost bounded.
- Retention: full-trace artifacts retained for 30 days (aligned with the incident review window) and archived to cold storage (GCS) for 12 months for cross-release comparisons.

Profiling cadence (recommended schedule)

1) Daily lightweight probes (continuous):
   - Metric rollups + micro-histogram snapshots every minute.
   - Purpose: detect immediate shifts in medians and p95.

2) Weekly focused traces:
   - 2x profiling windows (15m each) in staging matched to production traffic shape.
   - Run: guided by the benchmark suite scenarios (see integration).

3) Release gating profiling:
   - For any kernel or scheduler change that lands in main and is tagged for canary, run a release profiling session (two 15m windows) in canary. Must pass the profiling gate (no new anomalies at p99 and no unexplained error-rate increase).

4) On-demand deep captures:
   - Triggered from an incident or a scheduled experiment. Can be 30–120 minutes, must be pre-approved by runtime leadership if > 30 minutes due to cost.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

Preconditions: you are oncall or the owner of a flagged release. Have access to the profiling orchestration tool (profilingctl) and the benchmark runner.

1) Validate the alert: confirm Prometheus/Grafana alert and cross-check with product-level SLOs.
2) Correlate: use the request-tagged rollups to identify cohorts (model variant, seq_length_bucket, priority_class).
3) If tail signals are present, promote a profiling window targeting the affected shard(s) for 15 minutes (profilingctl start-window --shard <id> --duration 15m --cohort <tag>).
4) Collect kernel samples and GPU-side counters. Verify the sample set exceeds the minimum capture size (>= 200 kernel samples for statistical validity).
5) Run the local analysis pipeline (profile-analyze) to generate: hotspot table, costly-kernel-variants, and cross-correlation with dispatcher queue depth.

- Hotspot table: top 10 kernel variants by p99 increase vs baseline.
- Costly-kernel-variants: kernel ids with a >2x increase in per-invocation GPU time.

6) Triage: if a single kernel variant explains >40% of the p99 shift, open an RFC and page the kernel owner. If no single variant emerges, escalate to sysinfra and kernel scheduling owners to look for admission/queueing interactions.

7) Mitigation options (short-term):
   - Rollback kernel patch; or
   - Switch offending cohort to a fallback model variant; or
   - Temporarily increase admission control for the priority class to shed non-critical traffic.

8) Postmortem: capture the artifact id of the profiling capture and link it to the incident ticket. Run a follow-up benchmark against the microbench suite to validate proposed fixes.

Integration with benchmarking suite

- The profiling orchestration integrates with the benchmarking suite via a shared experiment manifest. Each profiling window can be replayed against the benchmark harness to produce a reproducible microbench against the exact kernel variants observed.
- Benchmark experiments to run after a profiling session:
  - sequence-length-scaling scenario at 4 concurrency points
  - KV-cache-warmup profile to emulate long-session traffic
  - scheduler-priority-noise injection to validate admission controls

Release gating and automation

- Any release that touches: kernel code, scheduler, admission controller, or the dispatcher must include a profiling gate. The CI pipeline will schedule a canary profiling window automatically and fail the gate if:
  - kernel_p99_execution_ms increases by > 10% vs canary baseline; or
  - kernel_error_rate increases by > 0.05 percentage points.

Runbooks (high level)

- Sev1: (p99 spike or error rate)
  1) Page runtime-oncall and kernel-owner.
  2) Run profiling window (15m) targeted at canary shard(s).
  3) If profiling confirms a single kernel variant: apply emergency rollback and re-run profiling.
  4) If not, invoke admission-control escalation to shed traffic and restore SLOs.

- Sev2: (p95 or queue depth)
  1) Perform correlation and schedule a 15m profiling window.
  2) Tune admission control thresholds for the affected priority class.
  3) Schedule a follow-up benchmark to validate tuning.

Known limitations and gotchas

- Sampling bias: deterministic sampling of top cohorts improves reproducibility but can miss rare degradations in low-volume tenants. Use on-demand deep captures for those.
- GPU counters missing on legacy accelerator drivers: in those cases we fallback to host-side timing and increase sampling rate for statistical confidence.
- Profiling cost: full-trace windows are expensive; long captures require leadership sign-off. Abuse of on-demand windows has previously consumed >30% of monthly profiling budget — we now require ticketing and attach artifact ids.

Operational ownership and contacts

- Scheduler & kernel owners: see TEAM-OWNERS index in the runtime-team wiki.
- Oncall rota: runtime-oncall (primary) and kernel-secondary (secondary).

Appendix: handy commands and queries

- Start a short profiling window (CLI): profilingctl start-window --shard canary-3 --duration 15m --note "p99-burst-investigation"
- Generate a hotspot report: profile-analyze --capture-id <id> --output hotspots.csv
- Grafana query for kernel p99: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_execution_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, variant))
- Baseline comparison job: bench-runner --manifest capture-<id>.json --replay --compare baseline-2024-11-01.json
